HJOB-CTX-G1.title: Tallowmarket research notes before the onsite
HJOB-CTX-G1.text:
TALLOWMARKET - MY RESEARCH NOTES BEFORE THE ONSITE
Last updated Sunday night. Sources: their engineering blog, the Series C press release, two podcast interviews, and a coffee chat with a former engineer (Wes Adeyemi, left in 2025).

COMPANY BASICS
- Founded in 2019 in Boulder by Renata Obi (CEO, used to own a restaurant) and Cal Whitford (CTO). HQ moved to Denver LoDo in 2022.
- Series C of $64M in February 2026, led by Harlan Ridge Ventures. The press release says the money goes to "payments infrastructure and expanding into the Pacific Northwest."
- About 140 people, roughly 55 in engineering (matches the job posting).

PRODUCTS I SHOULD MENTION
- Fieldpay (launched spring 2025): growers can get paid 2 business days after delivery instead of waiting on the restaurant's 21-day terms. Tallowmarket fronts the money and holds the restaurant's payment in escrow. This is why the Payments & Ledger group exists in its current form.
- Tallow Terms (pilot): net-30 credit for restaurants, currently piloting with about 300 restaurants in Colorado only. Renata said on the Supply Side podcast that Tallow Terms is "the riskiest thing we've ever built" because Tallowmarket carries the credit risk.

ENGINEERING - WHAT THE BLOG SAYS
- "Why we built Harrow" (post by Staff Engineer Maren Dahlquist, 2024): they moved from a single balances table updated in place to a double-entry ledger. Main reasons: they could not explain balance drift to Finance, and refunds were being applied twice when a webhook retried.
- Temporal adopted in 2023 for long-running payout workflows.
- A 2025 postmortem post: the nightly settlement batch overran by about 3 hours one night in November because of lock contention on the payouts table after a big Thanksgiving week. The fix was splitting the batch by grower region and moving to SKIP LOCKED workers. The post ends with "we still don't have good backpressure when volume spikes" - so it is still an open problem.

WHAT WES TOLD ME (coffee chat, take with a grain of salt)
- On-call was heavy in 2024; he thinks it got better after the Harrow cutover.
- Design docs really are the culture. Reviews are async, with a 48-hour comment window.
- The Payments team is 8 engineers. He said the manager is great at shielding the team but is stretched thin.

HOW MY BACKGROUND MAPS (talking points)
- Settlement reconciliation at Larkspur (312 to 41 monthly mismatches) is the closest thing I have to ledger work. Be honest: I have not built a double-entry ledger.
- Dockhand's transactional outbox is the same idea as avoiding the double-applied refunds in the Harrow post.
- Sparrowhawk (idempotency keys on PostgreSQL advisory locks) is directly relevant to webhook retries.
- Partitioning load_events by month is relevant to their volume growing from 400k to 1.5M entries per day.

QUESTIONS I WANT TO ASK
1. What does backpressure on the settlement batch look like today, a year after the November overrun?
2. How is the Tallow Terms credit risk modeled in the ledger - separate accounts, or a separate system?
3. What would success look like for this hire in the first 90 days?

THINGS I DON'T KNOW YET
- Whether the Pacific Northwest expansion changes the team structure.
- Who the hiring manager is (the recruiter never said).

PI-A:JD.title: the job description the user is targeting
PI-A:JD.text:
SENIOR BACKEND ENGINEER, PAYMENTS & LEDGER
Tallowmarket, Inc. | Denver, CO

ABOUT TALLOWMARKET
Tallowmarket is a B2B marketplace where independent restaurants buy directly from regional farms and ranches. Our Payments & Ledger group moves about $1.1B a year through escrowed payouts to more than 6,500 growers. We are a team of 140 people, about 55 of them in engineering. Our backend is Go on PostgreSQL, with Kafka between services and Temporal for long-running payment workflows.

WHAT YOU WILL DO
- Own services in the money path: escrow holds, split payouts to growers, refunds and chargebacks.
- Design and evolve Harrow, our double-entry ledger built on PostgreSQL, as volume grows from 400,000 to a projected 1.5 million ledger entries per day.
- Improve the reliability of the nightly settlement batch that runs at 02:00 Mountain Time and must finish before banks open.
- Lead technical design reviews and mentor mid-level engineers on the team.
- Join the on-call rotation, currently one week in six.
- Partner with Finance and Risk on reconciliation and audit requirements.

WHAT YOU BRING
- 5+ years of professional backend experience in Go, Java or Kotlin.
- Deep PostgreSQL knowledge: indexing, locking, isolation levels, and safe online migrations.
- Experience with event-driven systems (Kafka, Kinesis or similar) and idempotent processing.
- A track record of leading multi-engineer projects from design doc to launch.
- Clear written communication; we make most decisions in design docs.

NICE TO HAVE
- Prior work on a double-entry ledger or a payments platform.
- Experience reducing PCI DSS scope.
- Stripe Connect or Adyen for Platforms integration experience.
- Experience with Temporal or another durable workflow engine.

WORK ARRANGEMENT
Hybrid: in our Denver LoDo office Tuesday through Thursday; Monday and Friday are flexible. Relocation assistance is available for candidates moving to the Denver metro area.

COMPENSATION
Base salary band: $172,000 - $208,000 USD, plus equity and a 6% 401(k) match. This role is leveled at L5 (Senior).

INTERVIEW PROCESS
Recruiter screen (30 minutes), a 60-minute ledger design exercise, a Go coding session, and a values conversation with our Director of Engineering, Imani Castellanos.

Tallowmarket is an equal opportunity employer.

HJOB-CTX-C1.title: Tallowmarket recruiter screen notes
HJOB-CTX-C1.text:
TALLOWMARKET RECRUITER SCREEN - MY NOTES
Call with Jonah Pryce (recruiter), 30 minutes, last Tuesday. Typed during the call, cleaned up after.

ROLE
- Senior Backend Engineer, Payments & Ledger. Jonah said the role is leveled L4 right now "but it could flex" depending on the loop.
- The team owns escrow, grower payouts, refunds and chargebacks. He said Harrow (the ledger) is "the heart of it."
- He said Harrow does about 800,000 entries a day today and they expect it to roughly double next year.

WORK SETUP
- Jonah said the role is fully remote, with a trip to Denver once a quarter for planning week.
- Later in the call, when I asked about the team, he said "the team sits together in LoDo midweek, it's a great vibe." Not sure how that fits with fully remote. Need to clarify.

ON-CALL
- One week in four, "but it's quiet most weeks."
- The nightly settlement batch runs at 1 AM Mountain and "sometimes pages people."

COMP
- He quoted $150k to $185k base, plus equity. He didn't mention a 401(k) match.
- He asked what I make now. I deflected and said I'd rather understand the full package first.

PROCESS
- Next: a ledger design exercise (he called it 45 minutes), a Go pairing session, then "a chat with Imani."
- He said decisions usually come within a week of the final round.

MY FOLLOW-UPS
- Ask about remote vs office in writing before the onsite.
- Ask whether the level can be L5.
- Ask whether the band he quoted is for L4 or L5.

items.question: interviewer asked what i know about tallowmarket. give me 3 lines i can say
items.answer: Tallowmarket's a Boulder-founded, now Denver-based marketplace connecting ranchers and growers with restaurants, about 140 people with roughly 55 in engineering. They raised a $64M Series C in February 2026 led by Harlan Ridge, earmarked for payments infrastructure and a Pacific Northwest expansion. items.question: Why's that?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): So from what you've seen of us, what do you think is the hardest problem our payments team is dealing with right now?

NATIVELY: From what I've seen, the hardest problem looks like backpressure when volume spikes. The Harrow ledger rewrite and the Temporal payout workflows solved the balance-drift and double-refund issues, and the settlement batch overrun in November got fixed by splitting by grower region with SKIP LOCKED workers. But the team's own postmortem says they still don't have good backpressure under load, so that's the open one.
items.answer: The postmortem itself doesn't say why, so this is my read: the fixes so far were all about correctness, the ledger rewrite and the payout workflows, and the November fix was about lock contention. Backpressure is a different kind of problem, and it's the one that only shows up under real load.

items.question: How'd you validate that?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Tell me about Lanternfish. What was it and why did you build it?

NATIVELY: Lanternfish was a Rust sidecar I wrote at Cindervale. It exported per-pod DNS lookup latency to Prometheus, so we could actually see DNS as a first-class signal instead of guessing at it. The reason I built it was that checkout latency kept spiking and we had no visibility into where the time went. Once it was running, it showed that 31% of p99 latency on the checkout path came from DNS resolution. That turned a vague "the app is slow" problem into something specific we could go fix.
items.answer: I validated it by comparing the DNS latency it exported against the checkout p99 we were already tracking, and the two lined up: 31% of that p99 traced back to DNS resolution. I also ran it across the pods and confirmed the numbers held steady, not just a one-off spike.

items.question: Okay, three quick ones. First, tell me about a time you disagreed with someone more senior on a technical call. Second, how does the on-call you've done compare to what we'd ask here. And third, have you mentored anyone?
items.answer:
On the disagreement one, I don't have a specific blow-by-blow I'd want to put words in my mouth about, so let me tell you how I actually handle it. When I think a senior person's technical call is wrong, I don't argue the conclusion, I bring the evidence: the latency numbers, the failure mode, the cost. On Project Tern I was leading the rewrite of the carrier-settlement service into three Go services, and the calls that mattered were ones where I could point at the p95 or the mismatch count rather than just assert a preference. If the data doesn't settle it, I'll say I want to be wrong and ask what they're seeing that I'm not, and if we still disagree I'll commit to their call and note the risk. That's the honest version.

On on-call, I've been in a 6-person rotation at Larkspur, and I wrote the team's first set of 14 incident runbooks, so I've done the real thing, not just carried a pager. What I'd want to understand is your rotation size, your escalation path, and what a typical page looks like, because that's where the comparison actually lives.

And yes, I've mentored. On Tern I coordinated a working group of 4 engineers and 1 QA analyst over 7 months, which meant reviewing their work and getting them up to speed on the new services. I'd rather do that than just hand off tickets.

items.question: Tell me about Dockhand. Why a transactional outbox instead of just publishing to Kafka directly from the service?
items.answer:
Dockhand is the Kafka pipeline I designed at Larkspur Freight. It processes about 2.3 million shipment status events a day, and it writes to a transactional outbox table rather than publishing straight to Kafka.

The reason is atomicity. The status change and the event that announces it have to land together. If I publish directly from the service, the database commit and the Kafka produce are two separate operations, so a crash or a timeout between them either loses the event or duplicates it. With the outbox, the write and the event row commit in one transaction, and a relay drains the table to Kafka. That's what keeps the pipeline from producing duplicate writes.

items.question: Okay, but be straight with me. You've never actually built a ledger, have you?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): So from what you've seen of us, what do you think is the hardest problem our payments team is dealing with right now?

NATIVELY: From what I've seen, the hardest problem looks like backpressure when volume spikes. The Harrow ledger rewrite and the Temporal payout workflows solved the balance-drift and double-refund issues, and the settlement batch overrun in November got fixed by splitting by grower region with SKIP LOCKED workers. But the team's own postmortem says they still don't have good backpressure under load, so that's the open one.

NATIVELY: The postmortem itself doesn't say why, so this is my read: the fixes so far were all about correctness, the ledger rewrite and the payout workflows, and the November fix was about lock contention. Backpressure is a different kind of problem, and it's the one that only shows up under real load.
items.answer: Straight answer: no, I haven't built a double-entry ledger from scratch. What I have done is the adjacent work. I led the rewrite of a carrier-settlement service into three Go services, and I cut settlement mismatches from 312 a month to 41 with a nightly reconciliation job. So I know what breaks when money doesn't tie out.
